It is a fail-closed caller-input failure, not ledger damage, and there is no numeric error code to branch on.

What the "observation cursor" is: in the pinned Ordarium contract, `StateChangePage.cursor` is documented as the "opaque, filter-independent durable position of the last delivered change" for "incremental observation of committed state revisions after a durable position (ORD-BOOT-0)" (`node_modules/@ordarium/core/dist/src/types.d.ts`, `state.d.ts` `StateChangeFeed.changes(filter?, cursor?)`). A consumer persists that cursor and re-supplies it; that is the "stored observation cursor".

Rejection path in the exact pinned version (verified 1.3.1 in package.json, pnpm-workspace.yaml overrides, and node_modules/@ordarium/{core,ledger-sqlite}/package.json — all three agree):
- `@ordarium/core/dist/src/errors.d.ts|js`: `InvalidCursorError` → code `"INVALID_CURSOR"`, documented as "a caller-supplied change-feed cursor could not be decoded as a durable position (ORD-BOOT-0); distinct from LEDGER_CORRUPT … it fails closed instead of silently restarting from the beginning of the feed."

- `InvalidCursorError` is re-exported from `@ordarium/core`, so the integration can classify it by `instanceof` (consistent with the alignment charter's rule to map errors by type, not numeric code).

That file self-declares "Status: informational, not normative", and it is also factually off: `docs/engineering/07-ordarium-alignment.md` §1.2/§2 item 3 assigns codes 27–29 to `STATE_REVISION_CONFLICT`/`STATE_REF_NOT_FOUND` (state CAS/refs), not to cursor rejection. The exact pinned version is 1.3.1, and its shipped declarations define `INVALID_CURSOR`. The 1.2.0 references in the alignment charter are dated historical entries, not a competing interface authority.

## Answer

When a stored observation cursor is rejected, this workspace's integration should expect **`InvalidCursorError`** from `@ordarium/core` (the pinned `ordarium-v1.3.1`), i.e. an `OrdariumError` whose `code` is the **string** `"INVALID_CURSOR"` and whose message is "The change cursor is not a valid durable position; refusing to guess a resume point". It is **not** numeric code 27.

## Evidence (local provenance)

1. The "observation cursor" is the Ordarium state-change feed position: `OrdariumStateStore.changes(filter?, cursor?)` — documented in the shipped declarations as "incremental observation of committed state revisions after a durable position (ORD-BOOT-0)", with `StateChangePage.cursor` an "opaque, filter-independent durable position" (node_modules/@ordarium/core/dist/src/state.d.ts, types.d.ts).
2. The pinned contract defines exactly one cursor-rejection failure: `class InvalidCursorError extends OrdariumError { super("INVALID_CURSOR", ...) }` (node_modules/@ordarium/core/dist/src/errors.js:156-165, errors.d.ts:95-101), exported from the package index. Comment: distinct from `LEDGER_CORRUPT` — invalid caller input, not damaged ledger content, and it fails closed rather than silently restarting from the beginning of the feed.
3. Throw sites confirm the two rejection conditions: (a) a cursor that does not decode to base64url `{"c":"<digits>"}` (foreign/malformed), and (b) a decoded position above the ledger's change high-water mark — the restored/replaced/corrupt-ledger case. Both `MemoryLedger.changes` (core/ledger.js:50-68,281) and `SqliteLedger.changes` (ledger-sqlite/dist/src/index.js:382-393,770-787) throw `InvalidCursorError`.
4. The only local source naming "27" is `docs/engineering/notes/error-code-note.md`, which is self-declared "informational, not normative". `docs/engineering/08-source-precedence-policy.md` makes the published contract of the exact pinned version govern a dependency interface, and informational notes never override it. `docs/engineering/07-ordarium-alignment.md` (written against 1.2.0, i.e. before ORD-BOOT-0) maps "error codes 27–29" to the STATE_REVISION_CONFLICT / STATE_REF_NOT_FOUND family — a different family, so 27 could not be the cursor rejection.

## Integration consequences

- Classify by `instanceof InvalidCursorError` (or `error.code === "INVALID_CURSOR"`), consistent with this repo's rule that new Ordarium error codes map into the typed classification system and are never hard-coded by number (07-ordarium-alignment.md §3.2 item 4).
- Do not conflate it with: `StateRevisionConflictError` (`STATE_REVISION_CONFLICT`, the retry-safe busy family in src/effects/errors.ts — a wrong "27" classification would loop instead of fail closed), `LedgerCorruptError` (damaged ledger content), or `LedgerCapabilityRequiredError` (ledger lacks the `stateChangeFeed` capability — a different rejection reason with a different remedy).
- Posture: fail closed; discard/re-baseline the stored cursor rather than trimming it or silently resuming from position 0, and do not blindly retry.

Note: the workspace currently has no consumer of `changes()`/`INVALID_CURSOR` (grep is zero-hit in src/ and test/), so this is the expectation for the integration seam, not an existing code path.

submissionAttempts.body:
## What "the pinned dependency" is

`package.json` pins `@ordarium/core`, `@ordarium/host-kit`, `@ordarium/ledger-sqlite` to the `ordarium-v1.3.1` GitHub-release tarballs, and `pnpm-workspace.yaml` repeats the same overrides (plus `@ordarium/testing`). Installed artifacts agree: `node_modules/@ordarium/{core,ledger-sqlite,host-kit}/package.json` all report `version: 1.3.1`. (README/engineering prose citing v1.0.0/1.2.0 is stale context prose; it defines no competing cursor semantics, so it is not load-bearing here.)

## The surface in question

`StateChangeFeed.changes(filter?: StateChangeFilter, cursor?: string): Promise<StateChangePage>` — the "incremental observation of committed state revisions after a durable position (ORD-BOOT-0)" (`core/dist/src/types.d.ts`. It is deliberately *not* part of `OperationLedger`; reachable via `StateStore.changes` behind the fail-closed guard `supportsStateChangeFeed` (`capabilities.stateChangeFeed === true && typeof ledger.changes === "function"`, else `LEDGER_CAPABILITY_REQUIRED`; `core/dist/src/state.js`). Both pinned ledgers implement it and declare `stateChangeFeed: true`: `MemoryLedger` (volatile) in core, `SqliteLedger` (crash-durable) in ledger-sqlite.

Page shape (`StateChangePage`): `{ changes: StateRecord[]; cursor: string; hasMore: boolean }`. Unlike every other read surface (which uses optional `nextCursor?`), **`cursor` is always present** — reaching the end of the feed still yields a durable resume position for later commits.

## Exact cursor semantics

1. **Encoding (opaque).** `base64url(UTF-8 JSON)` of `{"c":"<decimal digits>"}` (`core/dist/src/ledger.js` `encodeCursor`; `ledger-sqlite/dist/src/index.js:722`, emitted at `index.js:418`). `c` is the **global commit position (`change_seq`) of the last delivered change**; `{"c":"0"}` denotes the start of the feed. Callers must treat it as opaque.

2. **Decoding is strict and fail-closed.** `JSON.parse` must succeed and yield a non-null, non-array object; `parsed.c` must be a `string` matching `/^\d+$/u`; `Number(c)` must be a safe integer `>= 0`. Any deviation throws `InvalidCursorError` (code `INVALID_CURSOR`, "refusing to guess a resume point"; `core/dist/src/errors.d.ts`). Both implementations are identical here (`core/dist/src/ledger.js:49-66`; `index.js:770-789`). Malformed input is treated as caller error, never as `LEDGER_CORRUPT`, and never silently restarts at 0.

3. **Resume rule: position inclusive, resume exclusive.** `cursor === undefined` ⇒ `after = 0` (deliver from the beginning). Delivery is strictly past the encoded position (SQLite `WHERE c.change_seq > ?`; memory starts at `index === after`). The cursor therefore denotes the last change already seen, and the next call returns everything committed after it — no duplicate of the last delivered change, no gap. A supplied but empty/invalid string fails with `INVALID_CURSOR`.

4. **Positions are real commit order.** SQLite uses `change_seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` (`migrations.js`), written **inside the same transaction** as the state revision CAS, so a committed revision and its observable position are never split and a rolled-back CAS leaves neither; positions are never reused. The v3→v4 migration backfills deterministic synthetic positions `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY namespace, key, revision)`, explicitly labelled migration order rather than original commit order; from v4 on it is true durable DB order. `MemoryLedger` appends an in-memory ordering entry (index+1 = position), which is honest only for its process-local/volatile durability.

5. **Global and filter-independent.** The cursor carries no namespace. `filter.namespace` only selects what is returned; the position remains global (both implementations say so explicitly). Consequences: (a) a cursor is valid across filter changes; (b) the cursor only advances to the last *delivered matching* change, so a namespace-filtered consumer whose namespace has no new commits gets back the same cursor and `hasMore:false` even though the ledger's global high-water mark has moved — "caught up" for that filter, not for the ledger.

6. **High-water validation (ORD-BOOT-0.1).** Before querying, both compare `after` against the ledger's own high-water mark — SQLite `MAX(change_seq)` (0 when empty; `index.js:579-584`), memory `#stateChanges.length`. `after > mark` ⇒ `InvalidCursorError`; `after == mark` is valid (caught up). This fails closed on a foreign/restored/replaced/shortened ledger instead of guessing or hanging. Concurrent commits only raise the mark, so a legitimately issued cursor cannot be falsely rejected. (Residual gap: replacement by a different ledger whose mark is equal-or-higher is not detected by this check.)

7. **Bounding, filtering, `hasMore`.** `limit` lives inside the filter (`StateChangeFilter.limit`): default 100, must be a safe integer in 1..1000 (`RESOURCE_LIMITS.maxStateChangePageItems`), else `TypeError`. The filter must be an object and `namespace` a string, else `TypeError`. Implementations fetch `bound + 1` rows and set `hasMore = rows.length > bound`, matching the doc "true when at least one further matching change already exists past this page" — filter-aware and a snapshot of the already-committed set, not a promise. On an empty page the returned cursor is the incoming `after` unchanged (0 if none).

8. **End of feed.** An exhausted feed returns `changes: []`, the same encoded position, `hasMore:false`, and retains that durable resume position indefinitely. That is precisely why `cursor` is always-present while the other read surfaces use optional `nextCursor?`.

## Decision and why no peer contact is needed

The semantics are stated exactly once (the core `.d.ts` contract plus `errors.d.ts`) and realized identically by both pinned implementations; the only divergence is durability strength (volatile process-local ordering vs crash-durable SQLite ordering), which changes how strong the "durable position" promise is, not the cursor's shape, validation, reset rule or filter-independence. No local source states a competing semantic, so there is no unresolved load-bearing conflict and nothing owned by `ordarium.main` that is missing. Note also that the similarly named `docs/engineering/16-boot-pull-spec.md` (PLMP-CTX-4) is about context boot/pull handles, unrelated to Ordarium's ORD-BOOT-0 feed; and palimpsest itself currently consumes only the overwrite/list state surfaces (`src/telemetry/state_persistence.ts` uses `store.list` + `nextCursor`), not `changes`. Local provenance analysis settles the question, so I did not contact the peer.

**Disposition: resolved** — the incremental state-observation cursor is the opaque, always-present, global `change_seq` position of the last delivered change: `base64url({"c":"<digits>"})`, validated strictly (safe integer ≥ 0) with `INVALID_CURSOR` on failure, used as a strict `>` resume boundary, filter-independent, and cross-checked against the ledger's `MAX(change_seq)` high-water mark so a cursor ahead of the ledger fails closed.

QUESTION: exact semantics of the "incremental state-observation cursor" in this workspace's pinned dependency.

PIN (verified, three layers agree on one version): package.json pins @ordarium/{core,ledger-sqlite,host-kit} to ordarium-v1.3.1 release tarballs; pnpm-workspace.yaml `overrides` redirect the same four packages to the v1.3.1 tarballs; installed node_modules/@ordarium/*/package.json report version 1.3.1 (ledger-sqlite schema: LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION = 4). So the governing artifact is @ordarium/ledger-sqlite@1.3.1 (implementation) + @ordarium/core@1.3.1 (contract types/state facade), spec label ORD-BOOT-0 / ORD-BOOT-0.1.

SURFACE: the cursor is `StateChangePage.cursor`, returned by `SqliteLedger.changes(filter?, cursor?)` / `OrdariumStateStore.changes(...)`. Types: core/dist/src/types.d.ts (StateChangeFilter/StateChangePage/StateChangeFeed) and core/dist/src/state.d.ts; impl core/dist/src/ledger.js (MemoryLedger) and ledger-sqlite/dist/src/index.js:382-421 (SqliteLedger).

EXACT SEMANTICS
1. Encoding/shape: opaque string = base64url(JSON `{"c":"<digits>"}`) (ledger-sqlite index.js:722-723 encode, :767 comment, :769-790 decode). The digits are the ledger-global `change_seq`, declared in the schema as `change_seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` in table `ordarium_state_changes` (migrations.js:163). Cursor content is not contract — callers must treat it as opaque and echo it back.

2. Position space: global commit-observation order per ledger, filter-independent (not per-namespace, not the subject revision number). The ordering row is inserted in the same transaction as the revision inside `compareAndSetState` (index.js:371), so a committed revision and its observable position are never split and a rolled-back CAS leaves neither.

3. Resume is exclusive and ascending: query is `WHERE c.change_seq > after ORDER BY c.change_seq ASC` (:395-410). Passing a cursor back returns only strictly newer revisions — no duplicates, no replay of the last delivered one.

4. Absent cursor = position 0 = full replay from the beginning (:386: `cursor === undefined ? 0 : decode(...)`).

5. `cursor` is ALWAYS present on the response (deliberate contrast with `nextCursor?` on history/list/stateHistory/listStates). On an empty page the returned cursor is the input position (or encoded 0 when none was given) (:415-419), so "nothing new yet" is a stable, idempotent resume point rather than an undefined marker.

6. `hasMore` is only a hint that >=1 further *matching* change already exists past this page (the SQL LIMIT is bound+1 and the namespace clause is applied before the limit, :395-410; `hasMore: rows.length > bound`). `hasMore === false` does NOT close the feed — later commits may appear; it is not a wait/end marker. The page is capped by `limit` (filter.limit) = default 100, must be a safe integer 1..1000 (`RESOURCE_LIMITS.maxStateChangePageItems`), else TypeError; a non-object filter or non-string namespace is a TypeError (:791-808).

7. `namespace` narrows only what is delivered; it does not change the position space. Because the cursor advances only over delivered rows, switching the namespace filter mid-stream while reusing an old cursor can skip revisions committed below that position. A stable filter per cursor is the safe usage.

8. Fail-closed rules:
   - Undecodable cursor (bad base64/JSON, not a JSON object, `c` not a `/^\d+$/` string, non-safe-integer or negative) -> InvalidCursorError, code INVALID_CURSOR, message "The change cursor is not a valid durable position; refusing to guess a resume point" (ledger-sqlite :770-790, core errors.d.ts:92-100). It never silently restarts from 0.
   - Cursor position > the ledger's global high-water mark `MAX(change_seq)` (0 when the table is empty) -> INVALID_CURSOR (:388-393, :578-584). Rationale in the code: the cursor is global/filter-independent, so validation is against the whole ledger, not the requested namespace's last sequence; concurrent commits only raise the mark, so a valid cursor cannot be falsely rejected, whereas a restored/replaced/behind ledger lowers it and fails closed. Corollary: any positive cursor against an empty ledger is rejected.
   - Ledger missing the capability (no `capabilities.stateChangeFeed === true` or no `changes` function) -> LedgerCapabilityRequiredError / LEDGER_CAPABILITY_REQUIRED via `supportsStateChangeFeed` (core state.js:9-11, :77-82). Both shipped ledgers declare it true.
   - Non-cursor failure modes: closed ledger -> LEDGER_CLOSED; dangling ordering row -> LEDGER_CORRUPT (LEFT JOIN deliberately surfaces it).
   - INVALID_CURSOR is explicitly distinct from LEDGER_CORRUPT: invalid caller input vs damaged ledger content.

9. Durability scope: on SqliteLedger (crash-durable, local-multi-process) the position is stored in SQLite, so the cursor survives process restarts and is a durable resume bookmark. MemoryLedger also declares stateChangeFeed: true but its declared durability is "volatile" and the position is process-local (comment at ledger.js:110-116: the order is process-local and the capability declaration is honest about it).

10. Migration boundary: v3->v4 backfills synthetic positions 1..n via ROW_NUMBER ordered by (namespace, key, revision), explicitly labelled migration order rather than original commit order; post-migration commits get real DB order continuing above the max (migrations.js:112-131). v3 had no feed, so no previously issued cursor is reinterpreted.

11. Honest limitation: the cursor does not carry ledger identity and is not content-addressed, so a pointer from a different ledger is accepted whenever that ledger's high-water is >= the position; the fail-closed check only catches a ledger that is behind.

DECISION RATIONALE (why resolved locally, no peer contact)
- The pinned dependency artifact is the load-bearing source for this proposition and is internally self-consistent: type doc (core/types.d.ts StateChangePage/StateChangeFeed), facade (core/state.js), and both ledger implementations agree on the exclusive, always-present, filter-independent, fail-closed semantics; SqliteLedger (the one the workspace actually uses) and MemoryLedger agree on the contract.
- The workspace docs' "cursor" material is NOT co-applicable: repo greps for ORD-BOOT-0 / stateChangeFeed / StateChangeFeed / StateChange outside node_modules return 0 hits. The local cursor concepts are different surfaces: orchestration `project.cursor = MAX(event_id)` plus the opaque viewCursor (`v1:epoch:eventCursor:viewGeneration`) in src/tools/controller.ts and src/serve.ts, projection cursors (last_applied_event_id in src/state/event_store.ts), and the *other* Ordarium cursor family consumed by src/telemetry/state_persistence.ts:64-71 (`store.list(...).nextCursor`, a per-subject pagination cursor that terminates with undefined). None of these state the change-feed cursor's semantics, so there is no genuine cross-source conflict and no missing resolution owned by the peer.
- The only version discrepancy found (docs/engineering/07-ordarium-alignment.md's latest recorded pin is 1.2.0, while package.json/overrides/installed packages are 1.3.1) is a stale alignment-history record, not a semantic claim about the feed; it is not co-applicable to this proposition. The pin itself is unambiguous (1.3.1).

NET: the incremental state-observation cursor is an opaque, per-ledger, global commit-position bookmark (base64url of {"c":"<change_seq digits>"}), resumed strictly-after in ascending commit order, always returned (idempotent at end-of-feed), filter-independent, and fail-closed with INVALID_CURSOR when undecodable or ahead of the ledger's global MAX(change_seq).

In-code comment: "the cursor is a **global, filter-independent position**, so this compares against the whole ledger, not the requested namespace's last sequence." Ordering row insertion and the revision CAS happen in the **same transaction** (atomic: a committed revision and its observable position are never split; rollback leaves neither).
4. **Volatile ledger agrees.** `@ordarium/core/dist/src/ledger.js` `MemoryLedger.changes()` uses one `#stateChanges` array, "positions are contiguous 1..n", and validates against the whole array length.
5. **Schema line.** `LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION = 4`; the v3→v4 migration (`migrateFromV3`) backfills global positions with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY namespace, key, revision)`, explicitly labelled **migration order rather than original commit order**, after which `AUTOINCREMENT` continues.

## Why Record A, not Record B

Surface: `changes(filter? = {namespace?, limit?}, cursor?): Promise<{changes: StateRecord[]; cursor: string; hasMore: boolean}>`, reached via `createStateStore(...).changes()` (delegates) or ledger.changes directly. It is a declared capability (`LedgerCapabilities.stateChangeFeed`); `supportsStateChangeFeed()` gates it and a ledger without it fails closed with LEDGER_CAPABILITY_REQUIRED. Both MemoryLedger and SqliteLedger declare it true.
2. Cursor encoding: opaque; base64url of JSON `{"c":"<decimal digits>"}`. Decoder (core ledger.js:50–73; sqlite index.js:770–789) requires `c` to be a STRING matching /^\d+$/u, a non-negative safe integer. A numeric `c`, garbage base64, arrays/nulls all throw `InvalidCursorError` (distinct from LEDGER_CORRUPT: caller error, not damaged content).
3. Cursor meaning: the GLOBAL, FILTER-INDEPENDENT durable commit position of the last change delivered on the page. SQLite assigns `change_seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` inside the same transaction as the state-revision CAS (migrations.js:163, index.js:368), so a committed revision and its observable position are never split and a rolled-back CAS yields neither. MemoryLedger mirrors it with a process-local `#stateChanges[]` (element i = commit i+1); the capability declaration is honest that this order is volatile.
4. Resume semantics: strictly AFTER the position (`change_seq > ?`, Memory slices from index === after), ascending. No cursor ⇒ after = 0. Because it is a "resume-after" mark, not an inclusive bound.
5. Always present: unlike the `nextCursor?` of the other read surfaces, `cursor` is returned even when caught up / empty — it equals the last delivered position, or the input cursor when nothing matched, or `{c:"0"}` for a cursorless empty first call. So the last cursor can be reused forever as a poll bookmark.
6. `hasMore`: true iff ≥1 further MATCHING change already exists past the page (SQLite: filtered rows fetched LIMIT bound+1 ⇒ rows.length > bound; Memory: a matching entry seen after the page was full). The namespace predicate is applied BEFORE the limit, so hasMore is about matching changes, not global ones. `limit` default 100, must be a safe integer 1..RESOURCE_LIMITS.maxStateChangePageItems (1000), else TypeError.
7. Filter: `namespace` narrows delivery only; it does NOT rescope the cursor's position space. Consequence (the key nuance): the same cursor is accepted under any filter, but switching filters while reusing a cursor skips changes that were committed at positions ≤ cursor and never delivered. The cursor is "filter-independent" as an encoding/validation space, not as a per-namespace bookmark; a consumer that changes filters must re-baseline or accept the skip.
8. Fail-closed validation (ORD-BOOT-0.1): before querying, `after` is compared to the ledger's current GLOBAL high-water mark — SQLite `SELECT MAX(change_seq)`, 0 when empty (index.js:580–581); Memory `#stateChanges.length`. If after > highWater ⇒ InvalidCursorError. Rationale (stated in the code): the mark is compared against the whole ledger, not the requested namespace's last sequence, because the position is global; concurrent commits only RAISE the mark, so a legitimately issued cursor is never falsely rejected, while a restored/replaced/shrunken ledger lowers it and the cursor fails closed rather than silently restarting from the beginning or guessing a resume point. Documented limitation: a DIFFERENT ledger with highWater ≥ cursor is not detected — the cursor proves a position, not database identity.
9. Ordering caveat: ascending durable commit order. v3 ledgers had no global order, so the additive v3→v4 migration backfills synthetic positions in (namespace, key, revision) order (migrations.js:106–135, LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION=4); only post-v4 commits carry real database commit order.

**Ordering guarantee: the durable ledger commit-observation order of the management-state change feed (`StateChangeFeed.changes`).**

The integration this workspace embodies (Ordarium's host-facing boundary, whose first real consumer is Palimpsest) exposes exactly one ordering guarantee. It is the **durable ledger commit-observation order** ("持久的账本提交观测序"): a **total, ascending order over every committed management-state revision within a single ledger**, independent of filter/namespace. Contract wording: docs/13 §11 ("跨主体按持久账本提交观测序增量读取已提交修订"); frozen in docs/research/ORD-BOOT-0-state-change-feed-spec.md §3; encoded in packages/core/src/types.ts:205-212 ("committed state revisions in durable ledger commit-observation order, ascending").

**How the order is defined (LOAD-BEARING):**
- Order key = `change_seq`, `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` in metadata-only table `ordarium_state_changes` (no payload copy; the sole semantic truth stays `ordarium_state_revisions`). The position is assigned by the storage engine **inside the same transaction as the state CAS** (packages/ledger-sqlite/src/index.ts:481-489).
- Hence: monotonic, never reused, crash-atomic. `StateRevisionCommitted ⇔ eventually observable` (SCF-INV-1) and `FailedStateCAS ⇒ NoFeedChange` (SCF-INV-2; failed CAS / rollback leaves no position).
- Read shape: `WHERE change_seq > ? [AND namespace = ?] ORDER BY change_seq ASC LIMIT ?` (packages/ledger-sqlite/src/index.ts:508-527). Cursor is opaque base64url, global and filter-independent, durable across process restart / DB reopen, and always returned (also at the caught-up edge).
- Delivery semantics: `AtLeastOnceObservation + DurableCursor + IdempotentConsumerPossible`; page-size-invariant traversal with no gaps and no duplicates (conformance assertion: packages/testing/src/stateLedger.ts:222). Ordering correctness holds across independent local SQLite clients on the same file (SCF-INV-7).

**Decision rationale (why this and not alternatives):**
- `written_at` was rejected as an order source: multi-writer clock skew, equal timestamps, mock/non-monotonic clocks make `writtenAt_i < writtenAt_j ⇏ commit_i < commit_j`; it is metadata only, not a coordination clock.
- The implicit SQLite `rowid` was rejected as a public/stable identity: `VACUUM` or table rebuild can reorder it.
- `Date.now()`/in-process counters/UUID or lexicographic ordering were rejected as non-authoritative.
- Therefore the only honest choice was a storage-engine-assigned, transaction-scoped, persistent sequence (Option B; Option A, adding a column to the STRICT revisions table, rejected for rebuild/migration risk).

**Explicit scope limits (do not over-claim):**
- It is **not** a causal order, wall-clock order, or business-priority order; it says only "committed/observable before-after" in ledger terms.
- It is **not** a global order across independent ledgers/databases/hosts (no distributed consensus, network-FS or multi-host guarantee). `LedgerIdentityBinding` is explicitly DEFER, so a cursor imported from a different, lower-watermark database is undetectable (documented known limitation, ORD-BOOT-0.1 §9).
- It is **not** exactly-once and carries no ack/consumer offsets/delivery leases/mailbox. `MemoryLedger`'s order is process-local/volatile; only `SqliteLedger` is crash-durable.
- **Historical caveat:** the v3→v4 backfill assigns a deterministic *synthetic* position ordered by `(namespace ASC, key ASC, revision ASC)`, explicitly **not** the original commit order (v3 never recorded it). The real durable commit order applies only to commits at/after schema v4 (packages/ledger-sqlite/src/migrations.ts:138-166).
- For contrast, the operation side promises no execution ordering — only stable operation identity, revision CAS, lease/fencing; `history` is ordered per-operation by `semanticRevision` and `list()` by `(updatedAt DESC, operationId DESC)`, which are read-surface orders, not this integration's ordering guarantee.

QUESTION: exact semantics of the incremental state-observation cursor in this workspace's pinned dependency.

WHAT IS PINNED (provenance). package.json pins four @ordarium/* release tarballs at tag ordarium-v1.3.1; pnpm-workspace.yaml `overrides` redirects the same four to the same v1.3.1 URLs; installed node_modules/@ordarium/core/package.json and node_modules/@ordarium/ledger-sqlite/package.json both say "version": "1.3.1". So the authoritative artifact = @ordarium/core 1.3.1 + @ordarium/ledger-sqlite 1.3.1 as vendored locally. The only local prose about Ordarium versions is non-load-bearing and stale (README links the release *page* ordarium-v1.0.0; the pnpm-workspace comment cites a packed inter-dep "@ordarium/core \"1.1.0\"" while installed ledger-sqlite declares 1.3.1). None of these texts states cursor semantics, so they raise no semantic conflict.

THE CURSOR IN QUESTION. It is `StateChangePage.cursor` returned by `changes(filter?, cursor?)` of the StateChangeFeed capability (ORD-BOOT-0), surfaced as `OrdariumStateStore.changes(...)` (core state.js). It is an ADDITIVE capability, not the base port: `OperationLedger` (core types.d.ts) has no `changes`; a `StateChangeFeed` interface declares it; `capabilities.stateChangeFeed?` declares support; `supportsStateChangeFeed()` requires `capabilities.stateChangeFeed === true && typeof ledger.changes === "function"`; without it `StateStore.changes` fails closed with LEDGER_CAPABILITY_REQUIRED. It must not be conflated with the dependency's other cursors: operation `list` `{u,o}`, operation `history` `{r}`, `stateHistory` `{r}`, `listStates`/`listStatesReferencing` subject cursors — all of those expose optional `nextCursor?` and none is global.

EXACT SEMANTICS (verified in both implementations):
1. Shape/encoding — opaque token = base64url of UTF-8 JSON `{"c":"<digits>"}`. Decoding requires a JSON object (not null/array), `c` a string matching /^\d+$/, `Number(c)` a non-negative safe integer; any violation throws InvalidCursorError (code INVALID_CURSOR), deliberately distinct from LEDGER_CORRUPT because it is invalid caller input, and it fails closed instead of silently restarting at 0.
2. Position meaning — a GLOBAL (all-namespaces), durable, monotonic COMMIT-observation position assigned when a state revision is committed. In SqliteLedger it is `ordarium_state_changes.change_seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`, inserted in the SAME transaction as the revision (and refs): "a committed revision and its observable change position are never split, and a rolled-back CAS leaves neither"; order = db commit order. It is NOT the per-subject StateRecord.revision (first write = revision 1) and NOT a per-namespace sequence.
3. Resume — omitted cursor = start after position 0 (whole feed). A call returns committed revisions with position > cursor, ascending, at most filter.limit items (default 100; must be a safe integer in 1..1000 = RESOURCE_LIMITS.maxStateChangePageItems, else TypeError).
4. Always-present position — `cursor` is non-optional (unlike `nextCursor?` elsewhere): it is the position of the last delivered change, or the input position unchanged when the page is empty. Reaching end-of-feed still yields a durable resume position (a first no-cursor call on an empty feed returns the encoding of 0).
5. hasMore — true iff at least one further MATCHING change already exists past this page (sqlite: rows.length > bound; memory: set when the page fills and another matching entry exists).
6. Namespace filter — filter.namespace narrows which revisions are materialized; it does NOT partition the cursor space. Because the query is `change_seq > cursor` ordered globally, the returned cursor may advance across other namespaces' positions; that is harmless (they were never of interest) and is exactly what "filter-independent" means.
7. Fail-closed validation (ORD-BOOT-0.1) — if cursor > MAX(change_seq) over the WHOLE ordarium_state_changes table (0 when empty), `changes` throws InvalidCursorError, even when the cursor exceeds only the requested namespace's last sequence. In-code rationale: because positions are global, comparing against a namespace's own last sequence would be wrong; commits only ever RAISE the mark, so a valid cursor can never be falsely rejected, while a restored/replaced/reverted ledger LOWERS it, and an out-of-range position is a foreign/restored/corrupt cursor that must fail closed rather than guess a resume point. It is a one-sided range check: in-range positions are accepted, and nothing validates that a position "belongs to" the namespace (it cannot).
8. Migration caveat — LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION = 4. The v3→v4 migration backfills positions with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY namespace, key, revision), i.e. deterministic MIGRATION order, explicitly not original commit order; post-migration commits get real db order. So "durable commit-observation order" is exact for revisions written at v4+, synthetic for backfilled pre-v4 rows.

DECISION RATIONALE. (a) Two independent implementations inside the pinned artifacts agree step-for-step — MemoryLedger.changes (core ledger.js; volatile, contiguous 1..n positions, high-water = #stateChanges.length) and SqliteLedger.changes (ledger-sqlite index.js; durable change_seq, high-water = MAX(change_seq)) — same {c} encoding, same default/max limits, same always-present cursor, same namespace semantics, same `after > high-water → InvalidCursorError`; the duplicated helper validators are equivalent. (b) The typed contract (core types.d.ts) states the same in prose ("Opaque, filter-independent durable position of the last delivered change"; always present; optional capability). (c) No load-bearing local source conflicts: the workspace's own code/docs contain no occurrence of StateChangeFeed, ORD-BOOT, .changes(, or stateChangeFeed (its telemetry layer uses store.list(...) + nextCursor, a different per-subject keyset cursor). Therefore there are not multiple unresolved load-bearing sources, nothing is peer-owned, and no peer contact/escalation is warranted.

ORDERING GUARANTEE: the integration exposes the "durable ledger commit-observation order" (持久账本提交观测序) of the revisioned management-state change feed (StateChangeFeed / ORD-BOOT-0, hardened by ORD-BOOT-0.1).

What the guarantee is
- The authoritative truth stays `ordarium_state_revisions`; the feed is a read projection JOINed back to it (no payload copy, SCF-INV-5 single truth).
- Order is the position `change_seq` of the ordering-metadata table `ordarium_state_changes(change_seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, namespace, key, revision)` + UNIQUE(namespace,key,revision) + FK to the revision row.
- `changePosition_i < changePosition_j` means "revision i was observably committed before revision j in this ledger". It is a total order over committed revisions of one ledger, returned ascending (`ORDER BY c.change_seq ASC`, `WHERE change_seq > cursor`).
- It is a commit-order total order, NOT a causal, wall-clock, or business-priority order. `written_at` is metadata only (clock skew, equal timestamps, mock/non-monotonic clocks) and the implicit `rowid` is explicitly not a public identity (VACUUM/table rebuild can reorder). The sequence is assigned by the storage engine inside the commit transaction, not by `Date.now()`, an in-process counter, UUID sort, or lexicographic order.
- Atomicity: the ordering row is inserted in the SAME transaction as the state CAS, so StateRevisionCommitted ⇔ eventually observable via the feed (SCF-INV-1) and FailedStateCAS ⇒ NoFeedChange (SCF-INV-2, sqlite_sequence rolls back).
- Cursor is opaque, global and filter-independent: `namespace` narrows only the returned set, never the position space; a page's cursor is the last matched position (input cursor on an empty page); a caught-up cursor stays valid and observes later commits (SCF-INV-3 / SCF-INV-4, no gaps, page-size invariant).
- Delivery semantics are AtLeastOnceObservation + DurableCursor + IdempotentConsumerPossible; no distributed exactly-once (consumers may re-read after a crash; the host owns "consumer A is at X").

Scope / honest limits
- Ordering is per local ledger, for the same OS-user trust domain; no cross-ledger, network, distributed-consensus, CRDT or global-transaction order.
- Durability of the order inherits the ledger: SqliteLedger is crash-durable/local-multi-process (order survives restart and reopen); MemoryLedger is volatile/single-isolate, so its order is process-local only.
- v3→v4 migration backfill assigns a deterministic synthetic order `ORDER BY namespace, key, revision`; this is explicitly a migration order, NOT the recovered original commit order (v3 never recorded it). All new commits after migration carry the real persistent order.
- ORD-BOOT-0.1 adds only validity/resource bounds (limit ∈ 1..maxStateChangePageItems; cursor > global high-water → INVALID_CURSOR) and does not weaken or change ordering. No ledger-identity binding exists (LedgerIdentityBinding = DEFER), so a cursor from a different ledger with equal-or-lower high-water cannot be detected.

Why this is the applicable decision
- Sources are co-applicable and internally consistent: docs/13 §11 (runtime contract) states "跨主体按持久账本提交观测序" and names `ordarium_state_changes` as the ordering authority; docs/12–18 outrank the research specs. ORD-BOOT-0 (frozen design) §3 fixes the ordering, and ORD-BOOT-0.1 (frozen design) explicitly `supersedes` ONLY ORD-BOOT-0 §5 (future-cursor behavior) and §7 (allowed limit domain), leaving §3 ordering in force. So there is no superseding or conflicting ordering rule to reconcile, and no peer-owned gap needing escalation.
- The design choice (assessment §2/§3, Option B) was made precisely because the four rejected alternatives cannot honestly carry a durable, gapless, restart-stable observation order: `written_at` (multi-writer/independent clocks), implicit rowid (VACUUM/rebuild reorder), a revision-row column (non-PK column has no DB-native autoincrement; requires table rebuild), and no existing stronger global primitive (operation history/list are per-operation or by `updated_at`/id metadata).
- Machine evidence agrees: `packages/core/src/types.ts` documents StateChangePage as "durable ledger commit-observation order, ascending (ORD-BOOT-0)"; `packages/ledger-sqlite/src/index.ts` inserts the ordering row in the CAS transaction and reads `ORDER BY c.change_seq ASC` with a global-high-water cursor check; the conformance kit asserts "changes must observe every committed revision once in durable commit order" and page-size invariance (`packages/testing/src/stateLedger.ts`).

Bottom line: the integration's ordering guarantee is a single durable, monotonic, per-ledger total order over committed management-state revisions, ascending by database-assigned `change_seq`, global/filter-independent at the cursor level, delivered at-least-once with an opaque durable resume position — and explicitly not causal, wall-clock, business-priority, cross-ledger, or exactly-once.

submissionAttempts.body:
## Conclusion

The "incremental state-observation cursor" in the dependency pinned by this workspace is the **state change-feed cursor** of Ordarium `ORD-BOOT-0`: the `cursor` field of `StateChangePage`, produced/consumed by `StateChangeFeed.changes(filter?, cursor?)` and surfaced through `StateStore.changes` (`@ordarium/core`), implemented by `MemoryLedger` (`@ordarium/core/dist/src/ledger.js`) and `SqliteLedger` (`@ordarium/ledger-sqlite/dist/src/index.js`).

### Exact semantics (pinned @ordarium/core 1.3.1 + @ordarium/ledger-sqlite 1.3.1)

1. **Encoding/shape.** Opaque string = `base64url(UTF-8 JSON)` of `{"c":"<decimal digits>"}`; `c` must be a *JSON string* matching `/^\d+$/`, decoded to a non-negative **safe integer** = a global change position. `{"c":"0"}` ⇒ `eyJjIjoiMCJ9`. Payload must be a non-null, non-array object. This is *not* the numeric graph cursor and *not* the `nextCursor?` cursors of the other read surfaces.
2. **Always present.** `StateChangePage.cursor: string` is mandatory (unlike `nextCursor?` elsewhere): a consumer at the end of the feed still holds a resume position. On an empty page it **echoes the input position** (or `{"c":"0"}` on first call), so end-of-feed polling is idempotent/cheap.
3. **Meaning/order.** Ascending **durable commit order** of committed state revisions; each item is a full decoded `StateRecord` (one entry per committed revision). SQLite position = `ordarium_state_changes.change_seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`, assigned by the DB **in the same transaction** as the revision CAS (a committed revision and its observable position are never split; a rolled-back CAS leaves neither). Memory position = 1-based contiguous commit index.
4. **Resume is exclusive.** The returned cursor is the position of the **last delivered** change; the next page selects `change_seq > after` (`>`, not `>=`). No re-delivery of the last change, and an empty page yields no progress beyond the echoed position.
5. **Filter-independent / global.** `namespace` narrows *delivery only*. The cursor is a **global** position and validation compares `after` to the **global high-water mark** (`MAX(change_seq)` in SQLite; `#stateChanges.length` in the memory ledger), explicitly *not* to the requested namespace's last sequence. Consequences: (a) changes committed in other namespaces can sit "below" the cursor and are never delivered; (b) with a namespace filter, `hasMore=false` can coexist with `cursor < global high-water`; (c) switching namespaces with the same cursor treats the new namespace as a new observation stream (pre-cursor changes there are skipped) — by contract, not a bug.
6. **`hasMore`.** True iff at least one further **matching** change already exists past the page (computed by over-fetching `bound + 1` matching rows). It is separate from cursor presence.
7. **Page bound.** `filter.limit` defaults to 100 and must be a safe integer **1..1000** (`RESOURCE_LIMITS.maxStateChangePageItems`, the fixed 10× envelope, ORD-BOOT-0.1); otherwise `TypeError`. A non-object filter or non-string `namespace` ⇒ `TypeError`.
8. **Fail-closed failure semantics.** Malformed/undecodable cursor, non-object payload, non-string/non-digit `c`, non-safe-integer/negative value ⇒ `InvalidCursorError` with code **`INVALID_CURSOR`** ("refusing to guess a resume point"); **and** a syntactically valid position **greater than the global high-water mark** ⇒ `INVALID_CURSOR`. It never silently restarts from 0. `INVALID_CURSOR` is deliberately distinct from `LEDGER_CORRUPT` (which is for damaged ledger content, e.g. a dangling ordering row). Note the guard detects a *restored/replaced ledger only when it lowers* the high-water mark: cursors carry no ledger identity/epoch, so a foreign ledger with equal-or-higher high-water is not authenticated.
9. **Capability gating.** `LedgerCapabilities.stateChangeFeed?` is optional; `supportsStateChangeFeed` requires the flag to be exactly `true` AND `changes` to be a function; an unsupported ledger ⇒ `StateStore.changes` throws `LEDGER_CAPABILITY_REQUIRED` ("a durable state change feed"). Both shipped ledgers declare `stateChangeFeed: true`.
10. **Durability is conditional on the ledger.** SQLite = crash-durable; `MemoryLedger` = volatile, positions process-local, so a cursor from a prior process fails closed (high-water resets to 0). The "durable resume position" guarantee holds only on the crash-durable ledger.
11. **Schema-version caveat.** SQLite ledger schema is v4. The v3→v4 migration backfills synthetic positions in `(namespace, key, revision)` order, explicitly **migration order, not original commit order**; only post-migration commits carry true commit order.

### Decision and why

- **Identification:** among all cursor-bearing surfaces, only the change feed is documented as "incremental observation of committed state revisions after a durable position" and is the only cursor that is *always present* rather than a terminal `nextCursor?`. Ruled out: `history` (`r` = semantic revision), `list` (`u`,`o`), `stateHistory` (`r`), `listStatesReferencing`/`listStates` (subject) — these are termination pagination cursors, not incremental observation; and Palimpsest's own `graph.project.cursor` (`MAX(event_id)`, numeric) — a different subsystem/contract, not a dependency cursor.
- **Pinned version = 1.3.1:** `package.json` dependencies, `pnpm-workspace.yaml` overrides, and the installed `package.json` of both `@ordarium/core` and `@ordarium/ledger-sqlite` all say 1.3.1. The README's `ordarium-v1.0.0` release link and `docs/engineering/07`'s dated 1.1.0/1.2.0 records are historical/stale and not co-applicable to the current pin (no lockfile or VCS exists in this snapshot; the installed dist is the effective artifact). The cursor feature is present and consistent in 1.3.1.
- **No peer contact:** the semantics are fully determinable from the locally installed pinned artifacts, so no load-bearing source is missing and no unresolved multi-source conflict remains for the dependency owner (`ordarium.main`) to arbitrate. The only non-local items are the Ordarium 1.3.1 release notes and the ORD-BOOT-0 spec text, but the shipped dist implements that spec and is self-documenting; nothing needed for the determination is absent.

## Conclusion

The integration represented by this workspace (Ordarium workspace 1.3.1 — the **Ordarium side of the Palimpsest federation bootstrap**, whose integration surface across the ledger boundary is `StateChangeFeed`) is governed by the **durable ledger commit observation order** (`持久账本提交观测序`).

It is a **total order over committed state revisions within one ledger**, defined by `changePosition_i < changePosition_j`, materialized by `ordarium_state_changes(change_seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, namespace, key, revision)`. The position is assigned by the storage engine **inside the same transaction as the state CAS** (`compareAndSetState`), so a committed revision and its observable position are never split, and a failed/rolled-back CAS leaves no position (SCF-INV-1/2). The order is monotonic and never reused. The read path is ascending `change_seq`, bounded pages, gapless traversal (SCF-INV-4), with an opaque, global, filter-independent cursor that survives reopen per the ledger's durability (SCF-INV-3); a caught-up cursor remains a valid resume position. Delivery semantics = `AtLeastOnceObservation + DurableCursor + IdempotentConsumerPossible` (no distributed exactly-once).

What it explicitly is **not**: not causal order, not wall-clock, not business priority (ORD-BOOT-0 spec §3); `written_at` is metadata only (clock skew/equal timestamps/mock/non-monotonic clocks) and implicit `rowid` is not a public identity (`VACUUM`/rebuild can reorder). It is also not the per-subject `stateHistory` revision order, nor the `listStates`/`listStatesReferencing` projection orders — those are separate read orders. And it is **not a cross-ledger / distributed total order**: the guarantee is per ledger (`MemoryLedger`'s order is process-local/volatile; `SqliteLedger`'s is crash-durable local-multi-process), and `LedgerIdentityBinding` (cursor↔database identity) is DEFER, so a cursor from a different ledger with an equal-or-lower high-water is undetectable. The first Palimpsest bootstrap consumer therefore uses a fixed coordination ledger.

## Why this one governs (decision)

1. **Precedence.** `docs/12–18` are the binding contracts; research/spec/`docs/dev` documents are subordinate (`与 12–18 冲突时以 12–18 为准`). The runtime contract `docs/13 §11` states the feed reads `跨主体按持久账本提交观测序`, names `ordarium_state_changes` + same-transaction storage-engine allocation as the ordering authority, and explicitly excludes `written_at` and implicit `rowid`.
2. **Supersession scope.** ORD-BOOT-0.1 `supersedes` **only** ORD-BOOT-0 §5 (future-cursor behavior) and §7 (allowed limit domain). ORD-BOOT-0 §3 (ordering) remains in force and is restated unchanged in `docs/13 §11`; the 0.1 hardening (`limit` 1..`maxStateChangePageItems`, `INVALID_CURSOR` for positions above the global high-water) leaves ordering untouched.
3. **No genuine unresolved conflict.** Apparent differences are not co-applicable: `docs/dev/11`'s "no subscription/push" concerns push/blocking delivery (explicitly a non-goal: no long-poll/SSE/WebSocket/IPC watchers), not this pull-based bounded observation; the v3→v4 backfill order (`ORDER BY namespace, key, revision`) is a deterministic *migration* order explicitly flagged as "not the recovered original commit order", so it does not compete — it **bounds** the guarantee, which applies to commits written after v4 (pre-existing rows carry only the synthetic order). Because resolution is local, contacting the peer is not required; the peer owns the consumer's cursor, not this guarantee.
4. **Machine evidence.** `packages/core/test/state-changes.test.ts` and `packages/ledger-sqlite/test/state-changes.test.ts` (SCF-A01/A02/A04/A05/A07/A10b), plus the portable assertion in `packages/testing/src/stateLedger.ts` ("observe every committed revision once in durable commit order", page-size invariance, fail-closed cursors).

**Bottom line:** the integration's ordering guarantee is a single-ledger, crash-durable, total order over *committed* state revisions, assigned transactionally by the storage engine in `change_seq`, consumed at-least-once through a durable global cursor — not causal, not wall-clock, not business priority, and not a distributed/global federation order.

## Determination

When a **stored observation cursor is rejected**, this workspace's integration should expect **Ordarium's `InvalidCursorError`, whose stable string code is `"INVALID_CURSOR"`** — a deliberate fail-closed rejection, *not* a numeric error code (in particular not **27**).

## What the "stored observation cursor" is

The term maps to Ordarium's state-kind **change feed**, the only surface in the pinned dependency described as *observation* over a *stored durable position*:

- `OrdariumStateStore.changes(filter?, cursor?)` — `@ordarium/core` 1.3.1 (`node_modules/@ordarium/core/dist/src/state.d.ts`): *"Incremental observation of committed state revisions after a durable position (ORD-BOOT-0)."*
- `StateChangePage.cursor` (`types.d.ts`) is *"Opaque, filter-independent durable position of the last delivered change"* — i.e. a position the consumer keeps between observations, unlike the `nextCursor?` pagination cursors of the other read surfaces.

Palimpsest exposes exactly this surface through `PalimpsestEffectsRuntime.state` (`createStateStore({runtime})`, `src/effects/runtime.ts`), which the telemetry state-kind path binds.

## The rejection behavior (pinned artifact = authoritative local source)

The pinned dependency (`@ordarium/core` / `@ordarium/ledger-sqlite` 1.3.1, `package.json`) rejects a stored observation cursor in two cases, both throwing `InvalidCursorError`:

1. **Undecodable / wrong-shape / non-safe-integer / negative position** — `decodeStateChangeCursor` throws `InvalidCursorError` (`core/dist/src/ledger.js:51–70`; same shape in `ledger-sqlite/dist/src/index.js:770–787`). Contrast: the *list/history* cursor surfaces throw plain `TypeError` ("Opaque state list cursor is invalid"); the change feed is deliberately different.
2. **A decodable position above the ledger's global high-water mark** (e.g. the ledger was restored/replaced) — `changes()` throws `InvalidCursorError` (`core/dist/src/ledger.js:281`, `ledger-sqlite/dist/src/index.js:393`).

The message is *"The change cursor is not a valid durable position; refusing to guess a resume point"*, and `errors.d.ts` states the intent: *distinct from `LEDGER_CORRUPT` — invalid caller input, not damaged ledger content — and it fails closed instead of silently restarting from the beginning of the feed.* So the expected failure is one throw, not a silent re-baseline and not a corrupt-ledger verdict.

## Why not numeric code 27

`docs/engineering/notes/error-code-note.md` claims the cursor-rejection failure "was surfaced as numeric code **27**". That note is self-declared **"informational, not normative"**, and it conflicts with normative local sources:

- `docs/engineering/07-ordarium-alignment.md` §1.2 / §2 (#3) maps the 27–29 error numbers to `STATE_REVISION_CONFLICT` / `STATE_REF_NOT_FOUND` — a state-write CAS conflict on a different surface, whose actual code is the string `"STATE_REVISION_CONFLICT"`.
- The pinned Ordarium errors carry **string** codes, not numbers; the change-feed rejection's code is `"INVALID_CURSOR"`.
- Both `07` §3.2 (#4) and `docs/engineering/08-telemetry-externalization-spec.md` §2 make the discipline explicit: map Ordarium failures **by `instanceof` (stable code), never by hard-coded numeric codes**. The note's "integrations classified it by that number" describes precisely the forbidden practice, so it cannot be the behavior the integration should expect.

## Boundary / non-answer

This is *not* Palimpsest's own freshness token. A stale `?viewCursor=` is not a failure at all: the server returns HTTP 200 with the full graph, `changed:true`, and a fresh `viewCursor` (spec 35 VIEW-INV-4/6; `src/serve.ts:249–261`), and the legacy numeric `?cursor=` is never rejected either. Those are presentation-surface freshness tokens, not stored observation cursors.

## Decision

- Expected failure: `InvalidCursorError` (`code === "INVALID_CURSOR"`), thrown fail-closed by `changes()`; catch/classify by `instanceof` or the string code, never numeric 27.
- Recovery implication: do **not** silently resume from position 0; a rejected cursor requires an explicit (deliberate) re-baseline after the ledger's provenance is established.
- Scope caveat: Palimpsest's current telemetry path consumes `list` + CAS `write` only (`src/telemetry/state_persistence.ts`) and does not call `changes()`; this determination is the contract to expect if/when the observation feed is consumed.
- No peer contact needed: the pinned dependency artifact is the authoritative local source for the exact shipped version, and the sole conflicting document is explicitly non-normative, so the conflict is resolvable locally.

submissionAttempts.body:
## What the cursor is

The "incremental state-observation cursor" is the **ORD-BOOT-0 state-change-feed cursor** of the Ordarium dependency this workspace pins: `StateChangeFeed.changes(filter?, cursor?) -> StateChangePage { changes, cursor, hasMore }`, reached through `LedgerCapabilities.stateChangeFeed` + `supportsStateChangeFeed()` + `StateStore.changes()`. The contract lives in `@ordarium/core` (`types.d.ts`, `state.d.ts/js`, `ledger.js`, `errors.js`); the workspace's actual ledger implements it crash-durably in `@ordarium/ledger-sqlite` (`index.js` `changes()`, `#stateChangeHighWater()`, `decodeStateChangeCursor()`; `migrations.js` `ordarium_state_changes`). JSDoc names it verbatim: "Incremental observation of committed state revisions after a durable position (ORD-BOOT-0)".

## Pinned version / authority

`package.json` pins `@ordarium/core`, `@ordarium/host-kit`, `@ordarium/ledger-sqlite` at the v1.3.1 release tarballs, and `pnpm-workspace.yaml` overrides redirect the packed inter-deps to the same release; the installed artifacts self-report 1.3.1. Workspace prose is stale (07-alignment last records 1.2.0; README links a v1.0.0 release) — version scope + manifest/installed-artifact precedence resolve that locally, so behavior is read off the 1.3.1 artifacts. These are internally consistent (types + both ledger implementations + codec limit + error doc + migrations), so no cross-peer resolution was needed.

## Exact semantics

1. **Encoding.** Opaque string = base64url(JSON `{"c":"<digits>"}`); digits decode to a non-negative safe integer. Canonical encoder emits `String(position)`. It is a *position*, not an event id, not a per-subject/namespace revision, not a timestamp. `""` is invalid, not "absent".
2. **What the number means.** A global, **filter-independent**, monotonic position in the ledger's durable commit-observation order over the revisioned state kind. In SQLite it is `change_seq` (`INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`) of the `ordarium_state_changes` ordering row, inserted **inside the same transaction** as the revision CAS — a committed revision and its observable position are never split, and a rolled-back CAS leaves neither. Every committed revision of every subject gets exactly one position (the feed reports revisions, not latest-only subjects). Absent cursor = `0` = "before the first commit". High-water = `MAX(change_seq)` (0 when empty) in SQLite; in the volatile `MemoryLedger` it is `#stateChanges.length`.
3. **Call contract.** `filter` must be a plain object; `namespace` must be a string if present; `limit` (inside the filter) must be a safe integer in [1, 1000] (`RESOURCE_LIMITS.maxStateChangePageItems`, default 100) — note it rejects 0, unlike the `nextCursor?` surfaces that clamp with `Math.max(0, …)`. Returns revisions with `position > cursor`, ascending, namespace-filtered, at most `limit`, each validated through the single core codec (dangling ordering row / damaged revision ⇒ `LEDGER_CORRUPT`).
4. **Return shape.** `cursor` is **always present** and equals the position of the last *delivered* change; on an empty page it equals the input cursor exactly (`0` if none), so end-of-feed still yields a durable resume point. `hasMore` = true iff at least one further **matching** change already exists past this page (LIMIT limit+1 probe). With a namespace filter, non-matching commits after the cursor are skipped and the cursor only advances to the last matching change; no matching change can be skipped by paging.
5. **Fail-closed validation (the load-bearing decision).** A cursor that cannot be decoded (bad base64url/JSON, non-object, `c` not a `/^\d+$/` string, not a safe integer ≥ 0) **or whose position exceeds the global high-water mark** raises `InvalidCursorError` (`INVALID_CURSOR`) — never a silent restart from 0. A position beyond the highest known commit can only mean a foreign/restored/replaced/corrupt ledger; concurrent commits only raise the mark, so a valid cursor is never falsely rejected. This is deliberately distinct from `LEDGER_CORRUPT`: invalid caller input vs damaged content.
6. **Availability.** `changes` is intentionally not part of `OperationLedger`; the capability is explicit, and `StateStore.changes` fails closed with `LEDGER_CAPABILITY_REQUIRED` unless `stateChangeFeed === true` and `changes` is a function. Both shipped ledgers declare true; `MemoryLedger` is volatile (order/cursor process-local, honestly declared), `SqliteLedger` is crash-durable/local-multi-process, where the cursor is a true durable resume position.
7. **Ordering provenance.** `LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION = 4`. v3→v4 (the ORD-BOOT-0 boundary) had no recorded global order, so existing revisions are backfilled with a deterministic synthetic `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY namespace, key, revision)` — explicitly *migration order, not original commit order* — and AUTOINCREMENT continues above it. New/v1/v2 opens get real durable order from the start.

## Decision / rationale

The determination rests on the pinned 1.3.1 artifacts, which agree point-for-point between `@ordarium/core` and `@ordarium/ledger-sqlite`; no load-bearing conflict remains, so no peer escalation. The workspace's own `cursor`s are a different subsystem and must not be conflated: `graph.project.cursor` (numeric `MAX(event_id)`) and `ViewCursor` (`v1:epoch:eventCursor:viewGeneration`) are palimpsest-side orchestration-graph fixtures served over `/api/graph`; palimpsest does not consume this feed at all — telemetry uses `listStates` + `nextCursor` (`src/telemetry/state_persistence.ts`, PLMP-TLM-1 §1). The semantics encode deliberate choices: one global commit position rather than per-namespace sequences (a cursor stays meaningful across filters and denotes the shared timeline, not a projection), an always-present cursor (durable resume even at end-of-feed), strict decode + high-water fail-closed (a restored/replaced ledger cannot silently replay or skip), an ordering row atomic with the revision (position ⇔ commit), and a capability-gated additive interface (source compatibility for existing ledgers).

DETERMINATION: The "incremental state-observation cursor" in the pinned dependency is the `StateChangePage.cursor` of Ordarium's `StateChangeFeed` capability (feature ORD-BOOT-0). The pinned dependency is Ordarium release ordarium-v1.3.1, i.e. @ordarium/core@1.3.1 + @ordarium/ledger-sqlite@1.3.1 (pinned at package.json:32-34 and pnpm-workspace.yaml:15-17; node_modules/@ordarium/{core,ledger-sqlite}/package.json both report 1.3.1). It is reached through the state facade as `createStateStore(...).changes(filter?, cursor?) -> {changes: StateRecord[], cursor: string, hasMore: boolean}`.

EXACT SEMANTICS
1. Surface/gating: `OperationLedger` does NOT contain `changes`; it is the separate `StateChangeFeed` capability. The fail-closed gate `supportsStateChangeFeed(ledger)` requires BOTH `capabilities.stateChangeFeed === true` AND a callable `ledger.changes`; otherwise `StateStore.changes` throws LedgerCapabilityRequiredError (LEDGER_CAPABILITY_REQUIRED). Both 1.3.1 ledgers declare the capability: MemoryLedger (durability "volatile", coordination "single-isolate") and SqliteLedger (durability "crash-durable", coordination "local-multi-process").
2. Token and domain: opaque string; concretely base64url of JSON `{"c":"<digits>"}`, where `c` is a string of digits decoding to a non-negative safe integer. `{"c":"0"}` is the canonical start-of-feed position. The numeric payload is a position in the ledger's GLOBAL commit order over state revisions - the `change_seq` column of `ordarium_state_changes` (INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, ledger schema v4) for SQLite, or the 1-based append index into the change list for MemoryLedger.
3. Direction and order: strictly-after (exclusive). A call returns committed revisions whose position is greater than `cursor`, in ascending position order. Omitting `cursor` means start at 0 (from the beginning). Using the returned cursor as the next call's input is the intended incremental loop.
4. Always present: unlike the `nextCursor?` pagination of `list`, `stateHistory`, `listStates`, `listStatesReferencing`, `cursor` is always returned, so a consumer that has reached the end of the feed still holds a durable resume position for revisions committed later.
5. Filter and limit: optional `filter.namespace` narrows delivered changes (absent = every namespace); `filter.limit` bounds items per page (default 100; must be an integer in [1, 1000] = RESOURCE_LIMITS.maxStateChangePageItems, else TypeError). `hasMore` is true iff at least one further MATCHING change already exists past the page (implementations probe one item ahead / LIMIT bound+1); it states current ledger content, not a promise about future commits.
6. Returned value and empty-page stickiness: the returned cursor is the position of the last DELIVERED matching change. If nothing matched - including when the entire remaining tail is filtered out - the returned cursor equals the input cursor (unchanged), never the global high-water mark. So a caller must adopt the returned cursor each call and, on hasMore=false, poll again later with it.
7. Filter-independence nuance: the cursor's coordinate system is global and filter-independent, so a cursor obtained under one filter is meaningful under another; but its ADVANCEMENT is filter-dependent because it stops at the last matching change. Consequently, switching the namespace filter while resuming from a cursor can skip changes of the newly selected namespace whose position is <= that cursor. Lossless incremental resume therefore requires a stable filter (or re-reading under that filter's own position).
8. Validation / fail-closed: a malformed token (bad base64/JSON, non-object payload, `c` not a digits-only string, negative or non-safe-integer position) OR a well-formed position greater than the ledger's current global high-water mark (SQLite `SELECT MAX(change_seq) AS max_seq FROM ordarium_state_changes`, 0 when empty) both throw InvalidCursorError (code INVALID_CURSOR, "The change cursor is not a valid durable position; refusing to guess a resume point"). It is never clamped to the end and never silently restarted from 0. The high-water comparison is against the whole ledger, not the requested namespace, so concurrent commits only raise the mark (a valid cursor cannot be falsely rejected) while a restored/replaced ledger lowers it and fails closed.
9. Durability/ordering invariants: in SQLite the ordering row (`ordarium_state_changes`) is inserted inside the same transaction as the revision row, so a committed revision and its observable position are never split (a rolled-back CAS leaves neither). The v3->v4 migration backfills synthetic positions in (namespace, key, revision) order - explicitly migration order, not original commit order - while every post-v4 commit carries the real durable database order.

NOT THIS CURSOR: palimpsest's own `projection_cursors` (contiguous per-project `project_sequence`, chain-tail validated against event_id/project_sequence/event_digest in src/state/*) is an internal event-log projection cursor owned by this workspace, and `graph.project.cursor` / `?cursor=` is a numeric canonical event position over palimpsest's own event chain. Neither lives in the pinned dependency. Palimpsest currently consumes the Ordarium state kind only via `list` + CAS (`src/telemetry/state_persistence.ts`); `.changes(` has zero call sites in this workspace.

DECISION: resolved locally; no peer escalation. All load-bearing local sources are co-applicable to the same artifact - the actually-installed ordarium-v1.3.1 tarballs (core 1.3.1 + ledger-sqlite 1.3.1), their declared type contracts (types.d.ts / state.d.ts), and the two independent implementations (MemoryLedger reference plus SqliteLedger durable) - and they agree. No locally present source conflicts, so the peer's authority is not required; per the boundary protocol, differing documents alone would not justify contact, and here nothing differs. The apparent tension between the docs' "filter-independent" wording and the code's "stops at the last delivered matching change" is resolved as a global coordinate system with filter-dependent advancement, which both implementations confirm.
